name: buttercream frosting
instructions:
beat 1 cup butter (room temp) until pale and fluffy (~3 min). gradually add 3-4 cups powdered sugar. add 1 tsp vanilla, pinch of salt, 2-4 tbsp milk or heavy cream until you hit the texture you want.

CRITICAL — ADD FAT SLOWLY / INCREMENTALLY (WHETHER BUTTER OR CRISCO): if you're melting the butter or shortening before incorporating (or using softened fat that's on the loose side), add it slowly and incrementally into the powdered sugar rather than dumping all at once. It's very easy to overwhelm the powdered sugar with too much fat and end up with a shiny/greasy frosting rather than a proper matte-fluffy buttercream. Start with less fat than the recipe says, whip it in, taste + inspect texture, add more only if needed. See notes.
notes:
powdered sugar, not granulated. butter must be room temp — too cold and it won't whip, too warm and it slumps.

=== ADD FAT SLOWLY / INCREMENTALLY — DON'T OVERWHELM THE POWDERED SUGAR ===

Whether you're using butter or crisco (see shortening note below), add the fat slowly and incrementally rather than dumping it all in at once. This especially matters when the fat is MELTED or on the softer side — the powdered sugar can only absorb so much fat before the frosting tips from matte-and-fluffy into shiny-and-greasy, and there's no walk-back from that failure. It's a one-way trip: too little fat you can add more; too much fat means starting over or adding a lot more powdered sugar (which throws off the sweetness).

Practical approach: start with LESS fat than the recipe calls for, whip it in, inspect the texture, add more incrementally only if needed. Recipe amounts are a target, not a floor — different powdered sugars absorb differently, different room temperatures affect the softening, and it's easier to correct from too-stiff than from too-loose.

=== CRISCO (VEGETABLE SHORTENING) INSTEAD OF BUTTER — THICKER, MORE NEUTRAL, SHELF STABLE ===

Swap the butter for vegetable shortening (Crisco or similar) — either partial swap or full — for a frosting that reads thicker, more neutral in flavor, and shelf stable at room temperature. The dairy in butter is what makes traditional buttercream slump in warm rooms and go off if left out; shortening doesn't have that problem, so a shortening frosting can hold pipe-work / decorated shapes and can sit unrefrigerated for hours without softening.

One of the only applications where vegetable shortening is genuinely the right pick — most cookbook recipes call for butter as the flavor and dairy-fat carrier, but here the goal is structural stability more than butter flavor, and shortening delivers on the stability axis in a way butter can't.

Tradeoff: less dairy flavor. If you want SOME butter flavor plus SOME stability, a 50/50 split works — half butter, half shortening. Same technique otherwise (room temp, beat until pale and fluffy, gradually add powdered sugar).

PRACTICAL PAIRING: this shortening version is what to reach for when the frosting needs to sit out (a party cake that'll be on a table for hours, transported to an event, etc.) or when it needs to hold detailed decoration. Straight butter buttercream is still the flavor pick for eat-immediately service.
